passageLocation.chapter: Impressions of an Indian Childhood: My Mother
passageLocation.openingWords: I was a wild little girl

text: I was a wild little girl of seven. Loosely clad in a slip of brown buckskin, and light-footed with a pair of soft moccasins on my feet, I was as free as the wind that blew my hair, and no less spirited than a bounding deer. These were my mother's pride,--my wild freedom and overflowing spirits. She taught me no fear save that of intruding myself upon others.

Having gone many paces ahead I stopped, panting for breath, and laughing with glee as my mother watched my every movement. I was not wholly conscious of myself, but was more keenly alive to the fire within. It was as if I were the activity, and my hands and feet were only experiments for my spirit to work upon.

assessments.conclusion: The underlying English text is outside the usual copyright term: Zitkala-Sa died in 1938 and UK written works usually remain protected for 70 years after the author's death.
Project Gutenberg identifies this English transcription as public domain in the USA.

rights.caveat: This autobiographical Dakota writing must retain Zitkala-Sa's authorship and cultural context; the record covers clean English text only, excluding later editorial matter and illustrations.

curation.context: In this recollection collected in 1921, Zitkala-Sa writes of her seven-year-old self and the freedom her mother encouraged.
curation.rationale: Freedom, wind, hair, fear, fire, movement and spirit give this childhood recollection unusual physical energy. The passage remains grounded in Zitkala-Sa's own account rather than presenting Indigenous experience anonymously.
